svg.aria-label: Security and TrustZone -- the veneer is the whole seam. an arrow from A to B means files in A #include a header owned by B; the number is how many of A's files do so (counted across libs/ and port/) down: ra8_nsc - to ra8_hal (33), ra8_nsc - to ra8_core (27), ra8_secure_app - to ra8_core (24), ra8_dfu - to ra8_core (17) ra8_ota - to ra8_core (14), ra8_dfu - to ra8_hal (8), ra8_devcfg - to ra8_core (8), ra8_psa_crypto - to ra8_core (7) in: none -- no library outside this set includes a header owned by any of it; sixteen edges leave and the eight largest are above. The load-bearing number is not an internal one: ra8_nsc - to ra8_hal (33). The veneers are thin on each other and thick on hardware, which is what a secure gateway should look like. The one edge into the secure app runs from the veneers and never back: ra8_secure_app includes nothing but ra8_core, so the S/NS contract is one-directional by construction. Three internal edges across nine libraries; the grey four have none. Derivation: every arrow is an #include of a header owned by the target unit. CMake cannot answer this -- libs/*/CMakeLists.txt are no-ops and consumers glob libs/ lib to /src/*.c into one object library, so there are no target_link_libraries edges to read.
